subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OP WITHDRAWAL OF CHAR0ES AGAINST COLONEL GEORGE DREW

speechtext:
On the orders of the day:
Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Minister of Justice): I desire to inform the house that the proceedings against Mr. George Drew of Toronto for an alleged breach of the defence of Canada regulations, based on a statement given to the public press by him on June 5 last, relating to the report of the commissioner who inquired into the dispatch of the Canadian expeditionary force to Hong Kong, were instituted on the advice of Mr. D. L. McCarthy, K.C., of Toronto, retained as special counsel in that connection by the Department of Justice. This advice had been concurred in by the legal officers of the department.
Mr. McCarthy has since recommended that, in the light of subsequent developments, these proceedings be withdrawn, for reasons which he has set out in a letter to me of the 9th instant. This further recommendation has also been concurred in by the legal officers, and I have accepted it and authorized Mr. McCarthy to discontinue the proceedings accordingly. I desire to table Mr. McCarthy's letter, together with the concurrence therein of the deputy minister of justice.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OP WITHDRAWAL OF CHAR0ES AGAINST COLONEL GEORGE DREW
speechtext:
Read it.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: If hon. members desire that the letter be read, it is as follows:

Defence oj Canada Regulations
Honourable Louis S. St. Laurent, K.C.,
Minister of Justice,
Ottawa, Ontario.
Dear Mr. Minister:
Re: Prosecution of George A. Drew.
When advising as to the prosecution of Mr. George A. Drew in reference to the statements made by him to the public press on the 5th day of June last, the following facts and circumstances particularly impressed me:
(1)	That this statement or utterance must be considered in its effect on others in the light of existing circumstances;
(2)	That it alleged that the findings of the commissioner were not based upon the evidence; and further, that findings were made without evidence;
(3)	That it alleged that secrecy was purposely imposed to hide from the public evidence of inexcusable blundering, confusion and incompetence;
(4)	That it alleged that there were bloodcurdling facts which the commissioner suppressed and which should have been made public;
(5)	That it alleged that the government withheld information upon which a finding could be made;
(6)	That the accused was a party to the inquiry having been appointed as counsel at the instance of the Hon. R. B. Hanson, the leader of the opposition in the House of Commons;
(7)	That the accused is an ex-army officer and must be aware of the necessity of secrecy in war time;
(8)	That he impugned the bona fides of the commissioner in holding the inquiry in secret.
In my view, the clear meaning of the statement is that the commissioner was corrupt or incompetent and that he suppressed or misconstrued the facts.
The commissioner is the Chief Justice of Canada and a member of the judicial committee of the privy council. Having regard to his long and honoured career on the bench and his well known ability to weigh facts, and his wide experience in the conducting of public inquiries extending over many years, it is quite unthinkable that he should be corrupt, incompetent or unmindful of all the facts presented before him.
In peace time these statements, while serious, have not the same effect as in war time. There was no doubt in my mind that under the circumstances, and considering the author of the statement, and the nation-wide publicity which the statement wras given, it would be likely to prejudice recruiting in this country and the efficient prosecution of the war.
As I have already said, the statement was given to the press, obviously for wide circulation throughout this country, and in fact reached the press in the United States of America.
The report in question is unquestionably a report on matters in which the public have great interest; and particularly the relatives of those in the armed forces.
Since first advising in this case, matters have developed which in my opinion are of paramount importance, and which must be weighed along with the considerations which influenced me in advising a prosecution. There has been a widespread demand by members of parliament and the public and the press for a full and free debate and discussion of the commissioner's report. That these discussions, either in parliament, by the public, or in the public press cannot be freely and fairly carried on, while these proceedings are in progress, is obvious.
This is well illustrated by a report in this morning's press. While discussing the Prime Minister's promise that facilities for debating this question w'ould be afforded to the house, the leader of the opposition, the Honourable R. B. Hanson, took the position that "the government has taken every means in its power to frustrate debate by withholding evidence and from time to time resorting to an alleged rule that a certain inquiry is sub judice".
No doubt the inquiry referred to is the preliminary inquiry that is pending as a result of the information that has been laid in this case. That is true that it is sub judice. It is a well-established and traditional principle of British law that there should be no comment on or discussion of matters relating to judicial proceedings while they are pending. It is plain that if the commissioner's report is to be fully discussed in parliament and in the press, as it should be, this principle of British law must inevitably be violated. Events that have taken place since the information was laid more than justify this conclusion.
On the one hand it is unfair to the public, members of parliament and the press that they should be put in the position at this time either to refrain from discussion of this important public matter, or to run the risk of committing a contempt of court, which is itself a breach of lawr. On the other hand, if these judicial proceedings are carried on while the debate in parliament and public discussion is taking place, it is obvious that the prosecution cannot continue in that freedom and independence that is so essential in our administration of justice.
Therefore, weighing the importance of free parliamentary debate and public discussion as against the continuance of this prosecution, at a time when matters affecting the carrying on of the war are of such vital and immediate importance, I am bound to come to the conclusion that it is in the public interest that this prosecution should be withdrawn and I so advise.
I am,
Yours very truly,
D. L. McCarthy.
Then there is a memorandum dated July 10, 1942, as follows:
For the reasons given by special counsel for the Attorney General of Canada, I concur in the opinion that the charge against Mr. George Drew under the defence of Canada regulations should be withdrawn.
F. P. Varcoe,
Deputy Minister of Justice.

speechtext:
The house resumed from Thursday, July 9, consideration in committee of Bill No. 64, to assist in the carrying on and coordination of vocational training-Mr. Mitchell-Mr. Vien in the chair.
On section 3-Minister may undertake projects.

subtopic: FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES-ADVISORY COUNCIL
speechtext:
The whole purpose of the bill is outlined in the various subsections of this section. The first purpose of the bill is indicated in subsection 1 paragraph (a); it covers the training of persons to fit them, by working at or on projects, for employment "for any purpose contributing to the efficient prosecution of the war whether in industry or in the armed forces". Under (b) provision is made for the training of persons who, I ' presume, have returned from the present war, of whom there are quite a number; under (c) there will be the training of persons recommended by the unemployment insurance commission; and (d) makes provision for the training of persons who, I take it, will participate in any conservation works which the government has in mind.
The minister should give some details of just how each of these training schemes will be carried out. If we are going to train persons first of all to work in industry, how will that be done? There are several schemes. If these persons are working in industry, you can have either vestibule schools attached to industry, or you can have technical schools equipped to teach young men to operate the various types of machines that will be required. I should like to know whether one
(Mr. Ilsley.]
or both of these methods will be followed, because any other method is not a very likely way of training people to work in industry. At any rate I know of no other method. We have had no explanation as to which of the two methods will be used in training men to work in industry.
If they are to be trained for the armed forces, how will that be done by the Department of Labour? I thought it was the duty of the army or the military authorities to give men training to fit them for the armed services. As to paragraph (b), "to fit for any gainful employment former members of the forces of his majesty domiciled in Canada," I am in accord with that. These young men coming back, discharged for one reason or another, should be trained, but I should like to know whether they are to be paid while training. If not, I suggest they should be paid; and, if so, I should like to know at what rates. Will they be paid according to the trade they are to learn, or will there be an even scale of remuneration all round?
As to paragraph (c), which covers the training of those sent for training by the unemployment insurance commission, that is rather limited, because it permits only of the training of young men who during the past two years have paid unemployment insurance for 180 days.
As to paragraph (d), the training of men for conservation work, I should like to know how that will be done. The universities all have classes for lines of conservation, one of which is reforestation. Are these young men to be trained in university classes in reforestation, or will they be sent out under foresters? The same will apply to flood control projects. Just what can they learn under such projects. Take on the Grand River; that is an engineering problem. To have permanent employment after the war, when we are likely to have a period similar to that which prevailed after the last war, I think the young men should be trained for more than one job. The more jobs a man is able to fill, the more trades he is able to assist at, the more likely he will be to have permanent employment. On project surveys there will be little possibility of training young men fully along the various lines of industry or engineering in connection with conservation or works of national importance. In Europe before the war, in quite a number of centres, there were excellent training schemes. They not only trained men but passed them on from the training centres into their positions. The minister is perhaps acquainted with the Sandvyk steel works in Sweden, one of the greatest undertakings of the kind in the world. I had long hoped that there would be some such scheme in Canada whereby young men, sons of fathers working in such plants, would be trained to work in 44561-259J
great steel works through graduating from the training school, vestibule school or technical school associated with the works.
When one considers that that single works has not only trained its men but built for them some 1,700 houses-that is before the war; there are perhaps many more now-it has something there that is worth emulating in this country. As a former workman I look upon the industry as being thoroughly sympathetic toward any scheme that will thoroughly train young men for jobs, and for permanency in their jobs, liking for their work and promotion in their work, because in those vestibule schools in those great works in Europe they are trained all along the line.
Will the minister give us a good outline of what he proposes to do? He has a golden opportunity to do something worth while, and I look to him to do it.

My hon. friend has covered a good deal of ground, and I am glad he did. There are three types of classes already in operation: pre-employment classes; technical schools, which in some cities are running twenty-four hours a day; and plant training under the direction and advice of the federal and provincial departments of labour.
My hon. friend mentioned the armed forces. With respect to what we call pre-enlistment training for the air force, last year we trained 15,000 men. They are paid, through the labour department, a subsistence allowance of $10 a week for single men and $15 a week for married men.

speechtext: And they are graduated

speechtext: Into the air force. We also trained 18,000 men for the army. The men are already in uniform and receiving pay and allowances given to a soldier. speechtext:
Diesel engines and those trades that are needed in the navy. My hon. friend will realize also the dearth of skilled men at the outbreak of the war. It is no use crying over spilt milk; the condition existed. With the tremendous expansion of the fighting
Vocational Training

forces and of industry we just had to face up to the situation, and I think the house and the country may be proud of the way in which both industry and labour, as well as provincial governments and municipalities, met an emergency and made possible the provision of training for men for the army, the navy and the air force, and of course for industry.
With respect to conservation, that is a matter which will have to be decided at the conclusion of the war. This bill, however, does provide for the establishment of an advisory council. It will be composed of representatives of labour, employers, veterans' organizations, women's organizations and educationalists to advise the minister on plans that may be necessary in the future.
I agree with what my hon. friend said about apprenticeship. I think the past attitude of the people and governments toward the establishment of systems of apprenticeship has been a tragedy. My mind goes back to the days when I was an apprentice. But in the last generation there has unfortunately been a great let-down of the principle of apprenticeship in the various trades, and in commerce also. It is true that apprenticeship has been maintained where trades have been highly organized; I know many that still continue to provide apprentice training with strict supervision by employers' and employees' organizations. They regulate the number of apprentices in proportion to the number of journeymen, and also the length of time that they consider necessary before a young man becomes an efficient journeyman workman. I think in a modified way the Swedish system of which my hon. friend spoke is in existence in this country. Those of us who have lived in industrial communities have seen the development of the apprenticeship system. I think it can be said that the two major railroads of this country have an apprenticeship system that is as good as any system anywhere. The trainees are largely made up of the sons of railway employees. I know in the city of Hamilton in which I spent the greater part of my life, in some of the great industrial establishments the majority of apprentices are the sons of men in the industry. That is all to the good; with that you get tradition and the love of the trade that is necessary to make a good tradesman. I only wish it was much more intensively developed throughout the dominion.
At the moment there are three provinces that have apprenticeship laws. I know more of Ontario, in which I have lived all the time I have been in Canada, where, through the cooperation of industry, the government and

the employees, there has been at least a foundation laid of what might become, with careful supervision and nurture, a really successful apprenticeship system.
I think I have covered pretty well the ground my hon. friend asked me to cover. As we come to the various sections of the bill I shall be glad to discuss the matter further.

speechtext: I commend this bill highly. It shows that the present Minister of Labour is willing to build on the foundation laid by the man who, in my judgment, was the greatest minister of labour who ever sat in this house, the late Norman Rogers, who knew youth and who during the years of depression planned accordingly so that throughout the length and breadth of Canada the dominion and provincial governments had their youth training arrangements in every province. It was often said during those years of depression by the youth themselves, and sometimes by their teachers also, that education did not count. We find that education does count, and when the Minister of Labour builds on a foundation like that laid by the late Hon. Norman Rogers he is building on a foundation that will stand.

Vocational training has been going on in the provinces for the past five years, practically on the basis proposed in this bill. I would mention one defect. Many of these young men from seventeen to twenty-five years of age left school early, through no fault of their own, and have not been able to pass that examination in mathematics, and so have not been able to take the vocational training. I discussed this matter with the man in charge in Nova Scotia, and he admitted that there were numbers of very capable young men who would make good mechanics, welders, sheet metal workers, or other good tradesmen, who could not pass the preliminary test. He suggested that if the provincial government, in conjunction with the federal government, would authorize those in charge of vocational training to start a class in mathematics, they could short-circuit the school course by about 75 per cent, and thus in about three weeks or a month a good many of these boys would get the necessary grounding in mathematics, pass the test and be routed into some trade. This is an aspect of the matter which will have to be dealt with in the future.
This bill is going to take care of things after the war, when hundreds of boys-they

Vocational Training
will be young men then-will be coming out of the army who cannot qualify under the regulations to-day. Some provision will have to be made to meet that situation.
There is another matter on which I have recently corresponded with the department. The minister knows the mining situation in Nova Scotia. He knows that there are hundreds of unemployed men there whose services could profitably be used somewhere else. There are restrictions to-day on gold mining and on the base metal industries, and in consequence there has been an undoubted shrinkage in employment. Many of the men who were engaged in these base metal industries are now unemployed, and it would be well if they could take advantage of this vocational training. My correspondence with the department on July 7 was based upon inquiries I had received from many unemployed or partly unemployed miners in Nova Scotia who were desirous of going into some other industry. They can be paid from $8 to $13 a week subsistence while taking a course, which means going some three hundred miles from home and leaving their family behind. Thirteen dollars a week is not sufficient.
I suggested to the department at the time that they should be on the same basis as soldiers and be paid subsistence allowance during the time they were taking their training. Mr. Thompson, who I believe is the man now in front of the minister, wrote me a letter in reply to the effect that in Nova Scotia, at least, some arrangement unofficially was in effect with a new shipbuilding plant there, where men could be employed, if they had an aptitude for that class of work, receive wages, and at the same time take some training in the shipbuilding industry. "Unofficially" may be all right, but you are not going to get anybody to leave his home and his family at $13 a week, when he is dependent, for putting the thing through, on the good will of the employer. If this is a feasible arrangement some definite understanding should be had with industries that they will be prepared to accept men and step up their earnings while they are taking the necessary training.
These are two things which the minister, with the latitude he has under this bill, will have to take into consideration and try to have some understanding arrived at. The non-essential industries are shrinking. Many men will be unemployed who are not fitted to go into war industry because they have no training. Arrangements will have to be made to train them, and their families will, have to be taken care of in the meantime.
The matter must not be left to the good will of the employer. There must be some definite arrangement.

Mr. Chairman, I trust what I have to say will be in your opinion related to section 4, subsection (1) (e) and subsection 2. In subsection (1) (e) provision is made whereby the dominion government may assist after the war in "vocational training on a level equivalent to secondary school level", and subsection 2 provides for payment on a fifty-fifty basis as between the province and the dominion.
So far as those regulations go, they will be welcomed by educationists and all others interested in education, and, I think will meet a real need. Certainly it is my hope that the provinces will be sufficiently cooperative and the federal authorities will be sufficiently generous to provide under this bill vocational education for the boys and girls of rural Canada and the small towns of Canada.
I am fearful of the fifty-fifty basis because of what happened under the Technical Education Act of 1919. While that act was in force, only the larger cities of this country were able to take advantage of it, with the result that at present we have vocational education in most of our cities and practically no vocational education in any rural community or in many of the small towns across Canada. I think the time is coming when the federal

Vocational Training

parliament will have to face the proposition of providing federal support for education generally, not merely for vocational education, and on some basis of need instead of a fifty-fifty basis. Manitoba, for instance, has not yet been able to avail itself of all the money apportioned to that province under the 1919 Technical Education Act; other provinces required a renewal of the time limit under that act before they could take advantage of the money apportioned to them. So long as the small municipality has to pay the cost of education, or the major share of it, and the province only a small portion, the dominion also will be called upon to pay only a small portion on the fifty-fifty basis, and the burden of education costs will still be levied on the real estate owners within the municipality. There is no reason to-day why real estate in a municipality should be taxed for the education of children. Children are not educated for the benefit of that particular municipality; they are educated to be Canadian citizens, and as such their education should be provided by the provinces and by the federal parliament rather than by the local municipality.
, I have before me a bill drafted to meet this situation in the United States. There the situation regarding education is practically the same as our own. The authority for education, the control of education lies within the power of the state; the federal authority has no more authority there than has the federal parliament of Canada. Yet here is a bill, read in the senate of the United States on February 11 for the second time, and then passed to a committee of the senate for further study. This bill provides for the annual payment by the federal government of the United States of $300,000,000 to assist in all branches of education down to the kindergarten, across that country, and that money is to be apportioned according to a formula stated in the bill, which will give on the basis of the state's need, so that the poorer states within the union will get the larger proportion of the grant. That, I submit, is the only common sense way to deal with this question of educational opportunity and educational equality.
As a result of our system of leaving education to the small municipalities, we have in Canada to-day 30,000 rural school-teachers, practically all of whom are receiving less than $1,000 a year; 19,000 of them are receiving less than $625, and 13,000 of them are receiving less than $520. That, Mr. Chairman, is the lowest salary paid rural teachers anywhere outside Canada in the British empire.

The minimum salary paid to inexperienced women teachers in any other part of the British empire than Canada ranges from $700 to $800 per annum. As a direct result of this, we will have in September from 1,200 to 1,500 of our schools placed in charge of unqualified teachers who have had no professional education. It is simply impossible to-day, at the salaries paid, to get professionally qualified people to go out into the rural communities to teach boys and girls. I consider that a national calamity. Where is the point in fighting for democracy if we are to raise, during the years to come, a generation of children who will come under the tutorship of hundreds of teachers who have no special qualifications for their jobs? There is not another part of the British empire where educational finance is left in any respect to be a burden on the small municipality. In England, Scotland and Ireland from 50 per cent to 80 per cent of the total cost of education is borne by the national budget; in Australia 100 per cent of the cost is borne by the national or dominion budget; in south Africa 100 per cent is borne by the provincial and dominion governments. We are the only part of the empire where we still leave education to be paid for by the local municipality, with the result that we get only the type of education that the small municipality can afford. It is my hope that under this bill our rural communities and small towns and suburbs-

speechtext:
The house resumed from Monday, March 9, consideration in committee of Bill No. 5, to provide for the reinstatement in civil employment of individuals who enlist for service in His Majesty's forces or who perform essential war employment-Mr. Mitchell -Mr. Yien in the chair.
On section 1-Short title.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF INDIVIDUALS WHO ENLIST FOR SERVICE IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext: Will the minister give an outline of what he proposes to do to carry out the purposes of this bill?

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF INDIVIDUALS WHO ENLIST FOR SERVICE IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext:
The bill is more or less selfexplanatory. It applies to the reinstatement, upon the conclusion of the war, of men-and of course that includes women as well-who have seen service in the armed forces, the merchant service, and also of the firefighters who volunteered to go to Great Britain and assist there. The bill is along similar lines to acts now in operation in the United States, Great Britain, Australia and New Zealand. The bill itself is a result of a promise made, I think, by the former minister of labour to the leader of the opposition that the original order in council embodying most of the provisions contained in the bill should be enacted as an act of this parliament.

The bill has been approved by the major labour organizations of this country, the employers' organizations and the Canadian legion. It has been before the canteen committee and has been amended in minor points to make its intended meaning more clear. As we come to the various sections of the bill, I shall be glad to make any explanations hon. members may desire.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF INDIVIDUALS WHO ENLIST FOR SERVICE IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext:
The minister is right in saying that this bill as originally drafted was brought down in compliance with a promise made by the Minister of Pensions and National Health. When the bill was before the house on a former occasion it was debated at great length. I have not followed its career in the committee to which it was referred, but I would assume that substantial changes have been made in the bill, judging by the reprint which I hold in my hand. It went to the special committee on canteen funds, and the definitions and interpretation clauses have been practically rewritten. I confess I have not before me the changes made, and they are not apparent from the reprint. I am pleased to see that in section 3 provision has been made for one right that I suggested, namely, the retention of pension or other benefits. I am glad that it has been decided that "service in His Majesty's forces shall be deemed to have been service with the employer", for pension rights.
Perhaps some member of the committee or the minister could'enlighten me as to whether section 4 has been strengthened, that is, the defences available to employers. I do not want to go into a discussion of any particular section, but I did look upon that as rather a weak provision in the bill as originally drafted.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF INDIVIDUALS WHO ENLIST FOR SERVICE IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext: That is paragraph (c)?

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF INDIVIDUALS WHO ENLIST FOR SERVICE IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext: Well, all the paragraphs of that section deal with the question of defences available to employers, any one of the paragraphs could be urged. I think the suggestions made in the committee have nearly all been adopted. I agree that the bill has been strengthened by the suggestions made during the discussion in the house. Section 4 has been strengthened to provide more protection for the returned man who has found it necessary to have medical treatment. Section 4 (c) was the contentious section in the committee,

Forces-Reinstatement in Employment
but it was found that this language best suited the purpose of the bill. The language is identical with that used in the British act.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF INDIVIDUALS WHO ENLIST FOR SERVICE IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES

What the minister is saying in that regard is that the committee was unable to find any language better suited to the occasion. Section 4 (c) reads:
. . . that, by reason of a change of circumstances, other than the engagement of some person to replace him, it was not reasonably practicable to reinstate him or that his reinstatement in an occupation and under conditions not less favourable to him than those which would have been applicable to him had he not been accepted for service with the armed forces was impracticable, and that the employer has offered to reinstate him in the most favourable occupation and under the most favourable conditions reasonably practicable-
I have no concrete suggestion to offer, because I dismissed this bill from my mind as soon as it was sent to the committee, and I really have not thought about it since. I do suggest, however, that this is a wide open clause. We can understand this part of it-

by reason of a change of circumstances, other than the engagement of some other person to replace him-
But when you come to-
-that the employer has offered to reinstate him in the most favourable occupation and under the most favourable conditions reasonably practicable

That leaves it in the judgment of the employer.

speechtext: If my hon. friend will read section 10 he will see that we have provided that an officer of the department may take proceedings, if necessary, where an employer does not comply with the intent of the bill.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF INDIVIDUALS WHO ENLIST FOR SERVICE IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES

Since we are dealing with the bill more or less at random I should like to ask a question with regard to the section referred to a moment ago by the leader of the opposition; that is, section 4 (c). Let me put a concrete case. Suppose a man was working as a mechanic before enlistment. When he comes back from the war the position of mechanic is no longer open. Can he say to his former employer, "Well, you cannot give me a job as a mechanic, I admit, but I could also be a clerk. I want you to fire this man," who may have been employed there for thirty years, "and give me his job". Does this provision extend to any position? Must the man get some job, or is it confined to a position of the kind which he left? If he was a mechanic, and should there be no mechanics employed in that plant when he
returned, could he demand that a position be created for him, or could he demand some other position at the expense of a man who had been perhaps twenty years in the service of that employer?

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF INDIVIDUALS WHO ENLIST FOR SERVICE IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext: I would say common sense would have to be the rule. To deal with the hypothetical case cited by the hon. member, let us go back to the railway organizations, where they have seniority in the different branches of the service. A railroad engineer or fireman could not come back and put out a station agent, a telegrapher or a clerk. In the main I think common sense will have to rule in that regard.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF INDIVIDUALS WHO ENLIST FOR SERVICE IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext: But the man might be a good enough clerk. Could he compel his employer to fire a man who has been in his employ for many years, in order to give him a job?

I think the minister is quite wrong when he says that paragraph (c) gives the magistrate discretion. What paragraph (c) does is to give the employer a way out within certain limitations. This is one of the defence clauses available to the employer. With regard to the point raised by the hon. member for Comox-AIberni (Mr. Neill) I would say that this statute would not give the right to a man to come back and bump somebody, to use the term employed by the minister, out of a job of another category. I do not think it was ever contemplated that that should be done.
There is another point that should be dealt with. I do not know whether this has been touched upon in the earlier stages. The crown is the largest employer of labour in this country, yet this bill does not apply to the crown. What is the position of the crown qua employer with respect to the reemployment of returned soldiers? I do not think we could legislate with respect to the crown in the right of the province. Of course the Civil Service Act contains certain provisions with respect to preference for returned soldiers, but we have omitted from this bill a most vital factor. I wonder if that came before the committee.

The interpretation of employer reads:
"Employer" in relation to any person accepted for service in His Majesty's forces, means a person carrying on any undertaking or service in which the person accepted for service had been employed for at least three months immediately prior to the date on which he was accepted for service.
And so on. But it does not include the crown in the right of the dominion. The minister should withdraw the bill and make it binding on the crown. I commend that to the committee. I should like to get some support for this position. This is a proper bill in the interests of the returned men. Many of these men may not be able to take a more onerous occupation because of physical unfitness. Why should we be legislating to compel the subject to perform a certain function and leave the government entirely free to do the reverse?
What is the situation with respect to men who have returned from this war? How many returned men from this war have been taken into the government service? I assume that the Civil Service Act still obtains with respect to competition, but there are many temporary positions; how many are filled by men who have been discharged from the forces because of physical unfitness? This situation ought to be dealt with in the bill.

speechtext: A civil servant is granted leave, and I suppose he would not lose his seniority rights. I cannot imagine the crown being less generous than a private employer. I should not think it necessary to have such a provision in the bill.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF INDIVIDUALS WHO ENLIST FOR SERVICE IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext:
I feel that as a member of the special committee I should say something with respect to this bill. The hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) was not altogether correct when he said that there was unanimity of opinion among the members of the committee with respect to this bill. Bill No. 5 is predicated upon order in council P.C. 4758, which was passed on June 27, 1940. This bill is the outcome of a request by the leader of the opposition that the regulations contained in that order in council should be embodied in a bill. This matter was discussed fully in the committee, and as far as I understand the feeling of the members of the committee they were divided on the question whether this bill should be turned down and the order in council allowed to function for some further period of time.
I jotted down some of the criticisms of the bill which were made by members of the committee. They are as follows:
Purpose for which act is framed is a worthy one but it is full of pitfalls.
If employers are worthy, and no one doubts their worthiness, there is no need for the bill.
The bill is not flexible enough.
It is overloaded with legal jargon.
Some sections could be worked only by bluff and not by prosecution.
Splendid opportunity to set up a bureaucracy of little value or importance.
This bill has been studied carefully, and I submit that it should not be allowed to pass but that the order in council should be administered for some time to come. We are told that it has been functioning well and that all complaints have been settled satisfactorily. The following recommendation was made by the special committee on pensions which sat the year previously:
It shall be the responsibility of the governor in council, in cooperation with industry and with all other classes of employment, to assume full responsibility for the reinstatement of all exservice men in the posts from which they withdrew on enlistment, or in some other form of gainful occupation.
That provision should have been embodied in this bill. As the bill now stands, there is no provision for placing men in some other form of gainful occupation. For that reason I believe it would be better to allow the order in council to operate a little while longer until we gain more experience. We could then build a bill upon the experience we have gained.

I do not think that we can do less than they have done in Australia, South Africa and Great Britain. I am glad to go to those men who have knowledge of and are interested in Canadian returned soldier affairs-the Canadian Legion, which speaks for a large body of soldiers in this country. The general principle of this bill has been approved by industry and labour and by a large body of public opinion. If I may say so, to the lawyers of the house, I cannot hope I shall ever live to see the day when a bill that is perfect will pass the house.

will not be necessary to set up a bureaucracy to set this bill in motion. We must remember that the order in council will expire at the conclusion of the war, but if you have an act on the statute book it can always be amended. This bill, like the legislation of the other countries I have mentioned, is "founded upon our experience of the last war and up to the present moment. It would be very fine, of course, to write a /Christmas tree into this bill. My hon. friend suggests that the government should guarantee employment to everybody. That suggestion is in a class by itself and: would need provisions of an entirely different character. The bill is simply to provide for the reinstatement of the soldiers who already had employment before going to the war. It embodies the policy of the government that employers shall take their men back to work. For 95 per cent of the employers of this country I believe it would not be necessary to have this legislation, because I believe the men will go back to their old jobs anyway if their jobs are there. This legislation is necessary because there may be some employers who will not do the right thing by the returned soldiers. It is a step in the right direction, and it can always be amended when amendments are deemed to be necessary in the practical working out of the act for the benefit of the men for whom it is designed.

speechtext:
With
what the minister has said I am largely in agreement. I am just wondering if there is some reasoning which applies to an order in council falling by the wayside after the war which might not apply to the provisions of this statute, but I do not think we ought to refuse to pass the bill on that ground. I have a very strong opinion that this is an interference with property and civil rights which it would not be competent for parliament to pass other than in time of war. But that time has arrived and we have to meet the situation as best we can.
Returning to the question of the crown not being a party to it, I find that this question was raised in the debate on March 9, when the minister made somewhat the same reply as he did to-day. I think upon reflection that is incorrect in part, but only in part. Permanent civil servants who have enlisted have been given leave of absence, but, as the minister very well knows, there is a large class of government employees, known as temporaries, who are not technically permanent but who have been on the payroll for years and years.
I have always wondered why, if they were necessary they were not blanketed in. I suppose there is a reason; that each adminis-

tration does not desire to recognize that a job which was created for temporary purposes should by a lapse of time, and by that alone, become permanent, although it would look as though they were permanent when you reviewed individual cases. A man employed in a temporary capacity does not get leave of absence. He has no superannuation rights; he has nothing. Some arrangement ought to be made whereby these men would be protected. The bill does not do that. It has a limited application; so far as its limited application goes, it is a pretty good bill, and I am supporting it. I think the committee did a very good job, probably as good a job as they could. I would not expect that there would be unanimity in the committee.
The question raised by the hon. member for Camrose (Mr. Marshall) is a very much wider one than is attempted to be covered by this bill. The objective he has in mind is a most desirable one that everybody should be given a job; but we are not yet a socialist state. We may be rapidly coming to it. If we do come to it, and these gentlemen have the opportunity to put into practice what they preach, they will find some difficulties in the way which are almost insuperable. You just cannot do these things on the spur of the moment, by act of parliament or in any other way. There is only one way, one big way, to provide employment in this country, and that is by the encouragement of private enterprise. I hope the day will never come when private enterprise will be wiped out. It is the one big factor that provides employment, and instead of tearing it down we ought to try to build it up after the war so that it will function once more.

I was a member of the committee that considered this bill, and I agree to a large extent with the remarks of the hon. member for Camrose. When it came before the committee I regarded it as premature. Under an order in council the Department of Pensions and National Health had built up quite a service with respect to the rehabilitation of the men who are coming out of the army; and in view of the fact that two other committees are considering and
Forces-Reinstatement in

Employment
going very broadly into the question of rehabilitation I thought it was too early to pass a statute at this time which definitely ties up this particular phase of rehabilitation with any particular ministry designated to take care of it. That was the bill in its original stage.
In addition to that, the original bill placed upon men returning from overseas the onus of coming back to Canada and proving their entitlement to a job. That has been corrected in this bill. But my fear about the bill is that it may interfere with arrangements which are working fairly satisfactorily. That fear may be groundless, nevertheless the risk is there. Many of the shortcomings of the blil as it went into committee have been corrected. I think the major disability was that the onus of proof rested on the man. An additional clause is provided which places the enforcement of the measure in the hands of the government. The minister who will be charged with the responsibility of administering this measure will have to lay charges against the employer who violates any particular section. I still regard this as premature. However, as a member of the committee, and one who was in a minority position, I accepted the majority opinion. In the light of present circumstances the bill, in my opinion, is as good as it can be. But we know very little about rehabilitation, or what developments will occur a year or two years from now.
As to the point raised by the leader of the opposition with respect to protection for employees of the government, I see under this bill the government in the position of employer. It is a matter of defining "employer". The situation is not confined to civil servants. You have to-day in this country many government-owned plants-one, which we had the privilege of going through a short time ago, having 16,000 employees. Many of these people will enlist or be called up. When they enter the services the government is their employer. When they come back from the war the jobs they vacated may not be there. Under this bill, as I see it, the government is morally responsible to find employment for them. That is another reason why I regard the bill as premature. The order in council is taking care of the situation as it exists at present. This bill does not go specifically, anyway, into that phase of the situation, and we may be in a better position a year from now to judge and legislate on it. However, the government still have the power to make regulations by order in council; they make them whether they have it or not.

speechtext:
When the bill was under discussion I referred to the limitation of three months or four months in section 4. Section 4 reads:
In any proceedings for the violation of section 3 of this act, it shall be a defence for the employer to prove,-
(a) that the person formerly employed by him did not within three months after discharge in Canada from the service or from hospital treatment following discharge in Canada, or within four months after discharge overseas or from hospital treatment following discharge overseas, apply to the employer for reinstatement.
I remember very well what took place after the last war. I was associated with a very large plant and, contrary to the opinions I have heard expressed, I found employers of that day very anxious to take back men who had worked with them before enlistment. I found that very general; certainly it was true of the plant with which I was associated. We took men back who were not able to accept employment within three or four months after discharge, and we took back many men after a period much longer than that. My knowledge of employers convinces me that the three or four months limitation will not prevent them from taking men back later than that. I remember one engineer who came back and who did not feel like starting at his old job after his return. He had been through many fights, had been blown up two or three times, had the experience of men who face fire and shell and bayonet charges and who suffer very seriously in consequence. It was nine months before he applied and he was taken on again. Even if he had not been fit after nine months he would have been taken on. I know of another man, a shipper, who did not return to work for over six months after his discharge. He was unable to do so.

With quite a number of machinists it was between five and ten months before their nerves permitted them to go on their old jobs. There was a chauffeur who did not go on for fourteen months. So I hope it will not be considered that with regard to employers-at least those I have been in contact with, who were mostly men who themselves graduated from the ranks of labour to the position of employers-the three or four months' limitation will prevent them from taking men back later than that, but I wonder whether there might be the odd one who would try to escape under that limitation. What does the minister think of that limitation?

speechtext: When the national labour supply council was in existence-that was the council of employers and employees-we discussed this matter from the angle my hon. friend mentions and came to the conclusion that three or four months was the most satisfactory approach to the problem.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF INDIVIDUALS WHO ENLIST FOR SERVICE IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext: Were many of the members of the committee former employees themselves?

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF INDIVIDUALS WHO ENLIST FOR SERVICE IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext: Yes. We had the chief of personnel of the Canadian Pacific Railway and on the labour side the representatives of the dominant organizations. There was no disagreement.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF INDIVIDUALS WHO ENLIST FOR SERVICE IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext:
I think we had discussion in the committee on that very point. At one stage the limitation read "one month." Much has been said about the impracticability of this bill; we had to have something agreed on. After considerable discussion we arrived at this three or four months as a compromise to make it workable from the point of view of both employers and employees. It was a step in the right direction. Section agreed to.
Sections 5 to 9 inclusive agreed to.
On section 10-Prosecution on behalf of employee.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF INDIVIDUALS WHO ENLIST FOR SERVICE IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext: I understood from one hon. member who was on the committee that if an employee found it necessary to obtain legal advice, that legal advice was to be supplied by the government.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF INDIVIDUALS WHO ENLIST FOR SERVICE IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext: Yes, by the government.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF INDIVIDUALS WHO ENLIST FOR SERVICE IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext: But only when the minister thinks a prosecution is warranted, they undertake the prosecution; free legal advice is not provided.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF INDIVIDUALS WHO ENLIST FOR SERVICE IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext: That is what I meant, if legal advice is necessary the government will supply the legal advice at no cost to the employee?

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF INDIVIDUALS WHO ENLIST FOR SERVICE IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext:
At no cost to the
returned soldier.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF INDIVIDUALS WHO ENLIST FOR SERVICE IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext: That section is not clear. According to my impression in the committee legal advice was not to be provided where the minister considered a prosecution necessary, but it would be where the employer would not listen to any other argument; if the employer would not recognize the claim made in due course and in conformity with the measure.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF INDIVIDUALS WHO ENLIST FOR SERVICE IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext: I think there has to be some provision for nuisance cases, that the decision should rest with the minister, as with other prosecutions under the crown. What I think would happen would be that the welfare officer or those charged with the enforcement of this bill would go to the employer and the employer would see the penalities laid down. In my view the number of cases that would go to the courts would be very small and of a kind that would require getting the approval of the minister before a prosecution.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF INDIVIDUALS WHO ENLIST FOR SERVICE IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext:
That is all very well, and apparently compliments are in order.
I agree that the minister is one of the most outstanding ministers of labour who have been in the house since I have been here. There have been only two. But when a man is away out in the wilderness somewhere and an employer would not reengage him, provided he conformed to the provisions of the bill, my impression was that the minister would automatically take action. It is all very well to say that these things cannot happen; judging by some of the hon. members I have seen who might possibly be in the government, anything could happen. A soldier should have this right, just as he has now a right of appeal in a pension case and is entitled to the services of the soldiers' advocate. That is his right by statute, and I think it should be my right if my employer refuses me my position, that I can demand a lawyer paid by the crown to prosecute my case.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF INDIVIDUALS WHO ENLIST FOR SERVICE IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext:
That was rather my understanding in the committee. At one time the onus was on the employee. There was considerable discussion. The matter of the soldiers' advocate was discussed, as mentioned by' the hon. member for Fraser Valley. Now that the matter has been turned around, with the onus on the employer, the onus is

Forces-Reinstatement in Employment
taken off the employee to institute action. There has to be some discretion in the department. We have to have faith in the department seeing that the employee receives justice.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF INDIVIDUALS WHO ENLIST FOR SERVICE IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext: I wish to support the contention of the hon. member for Fraser Valley. Previously the employee had to go and get counsel. Now he will have to put his case before the minister. My experience in trying to get things through these various government departments is that there is interminable delay.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF INDIVIDUALS WHO ENLIST FOR SERVICE IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext:
He will
go to the welfare officer in the community first, and that officer will take it up.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF INDIVIDUALS WHO ENLIST FOR SERVICE IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext: But he takes it up with the minister, and the minister decides whether the case warrants action. It will then come back to the advocate, and perhaps proceedings will be instituted. But if the minister does not wish to institute proceedings, the man will be out entirely. It is entirely in the hands of the minister whether or not the man shall have his case taken on by the government or whether he will have to employ a lawyer himself. The greatest improvement made in the bill in my opinion was instituting this protection for the employee. It seems to me it would be much more in line with what the committee wanted if it were made possible for the employee to have at his disposal the services of someone in the same position as the soldiers' advocate in the matter of pensions. It seems to me this complicates the matter more than ever.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF INDIVIDUALS WHO ENLIST FOR SERVICE IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext: Shall the section carry?

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF INDIVIDUALS WHO ENLIST FOR SERVICE IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext: No. We spent three months on a bill that apparently is not to mean anything, the plebiscite bill. Surely we can take a little time on something that is going to help the returned soldier. I for one am not going to be rushed, if I stay here for three months more.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF INDIVIDUALS WHO ENLIST FOR SERVICE IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext: You will stay alone.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF INDIVIDUALS WHO ENLIST FOR SERVICE IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext:
All right. Probably I would accomplish more if I did. As I see it, there are too many loopholes. It could happen. I know it would not happen with any of the parties represented in this house at present; but do not make any mistake, such things have happened in Canada before. This government might not be in power; it might be any government. There might be a very particular friend of the administration; I could name them, both on behalf of the official opposition, possibly some of the government side and even some on the
part of our friends down to the far left. I am very doubtful about any prosecuting that would be done in connection with any of these firms, to put a man back to work. We all know these things happen. I for one would not want to be 3,000 or 4,000 miles away pleading my case with the minister in charge at the time, asking that he prosecute a certain firm which refused to put me back at work. I think it should be mandatory, with all due deference to the minister. I am speaking as a returned soldier. I do not want to be accused, as the hon. member for Yorkton was accused, of saying anything that would deprecate what we are trying to do for the returned men in this connection, but why not be fair and honest about it? I am also a member of the Canadian Legion, a charter member, but unless you put some teeth into this bill I do not think it will amount to what it is intended to amount to.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF INDIVIDUALS WHO ENLIST FOR SERVICE IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext: I do not share the apprehensions of the hon. member for Fraser Valley. This clause as it stands automatically gives the soldier the right to counsel in the event that lie has to prosecute an employer.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF INDIVIDUALS WHO ENLIST FOR SERVICE IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext: Absolutely.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF INDIVIDUALS WHO ENLIST FOR SERVICE IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext: And I agree with the minister that there has to be a stop block somewhere. I cannot view this clause in exactly the way that it is viewed by the hon. member for Fraser Valley. In the event of a dispute with an employer under this bill a man is automatically given the benefit of counsel.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF INDIVIDUALS WHO ENLIST FOR SERVICE IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext:
Only if
the minister agrees.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF INDIVIDUALS WHO ENLIST FOR SERVICE IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext: I cannot see him not agreeing. After a case goes through the unemployment insurance and welfare offices and finally reaches the minister, I should think it would be very apparent that something is wrong.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF INDIVIDUALS WHO ENLIST FOR SERVICE IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext:
And the employee
would be starving.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF INDIVIDUALS WHO ENLIST FOR SERVICE IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext:
That is a bad angle to it.
Unfortunately you fellows are still making these regulations, and we will have to go through these slow processes of law until somebody else makes them.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF INDIVIDUALS WHO ENLIST FOR SERVICE IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext:
They will be
awfully slow, too.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF INDIVIDUALS WHO ENLIST FOR SERVICE IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext: Shall the section carry?

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF INDIVIDUALS WHO ENLIST FOR SERVICE IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext: No.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF INDIVIDUALS WHO ENLIST FOR SERVICE IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman. That is not to be the title, as I understood it. It is six o'clock, Mr. Chairman.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF INDIVIDUALS WHO ENLIST FOR SERVICE IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext: I suggest that we carry on until we finish. The house is under tremendous pressure, and so are the ministers. I think we should go on.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF INDIVIDUALS WHO ENLIST FOR SERVICE IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext:
I would appeal to the
hon. member. We are on the last section of the bill; let us try to finish it to-night and not call it six o'clock. We might carry on for a few minutes.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF INDIVIDUALS WHO ENLIST FOR SERVICE IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext: Veiy well; I withdraw my suggestion. But this is a most important bill, and I do not think it should be rushed. Not two members in this chamber can remember the title as it was read. Let us know what we are doing.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF INDIVIDUALS WHO ENLIST FOR SERVICE IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext:
The amended title reads:
An act to provide for the reinstatement in civil employment of discharged members of His Majesty's forces or other designated classes of persons.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF INDIVIDUALS WHO ENLIST FOR SERVICE IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext: What is the meaning of "other designated classes of persons"?

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF INDIVIDUALS WHO ENLIST FOR SERVICE IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext: At the moment it means merchant seamen and civilian fire fighters who have been called up. I know what is bothering my hon. friend. He thinks it refers to industry, but he can take it from me that it has no connection whatever with industry.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF INDIVIDUALS WHO ENLIST FOR SERVICE IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext: As I understand it, this bill has reference only to persons who were previously employed.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF INDIVIDUALS WHO ENLIST FOR SERVICE IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext: Absolutely.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF INDIVIDUALS WHO ENLIST FOR SERVICE IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext: Do you not think it would be well to include somewhere in the title words to this effect, "to reinstate individuals who were previously employed, and who enlisted for service"?

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF INDIVIDUALS WHO ENLIST FOR SERVICE IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext: The word "reinstatement" connotes previous employment.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF INDIVIDUALS WHO ENLIST FOR SERVICE IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext: Would these "other designated persons" include men who enlisted but who were taken from the army and placed in other employment, by virtue of their techncial training? Under the bill as it now stands I do not think they have any protection.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF INDIVIDUALS WHO ENLIST FOR SERVICE IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext: If they are taken from the army they are given leave of absence, and are still technically in the army.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF INDIVIDUALS WHO ENLIST FOR SERVICE IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext: No, they have been discharged.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF INDIVIDUALS WHO ENLIST FOR SERVICE IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext: I know of no such cases.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF INDIVIDUALS WHO ENLIST FOR SERVICE IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES
speechtext: I have had two people write me who have been discharged from the army and employed in industry, but there is no protection for them.

Amendment agreed to.
